entry: Highly corrosive mineral acid, HNO₃. The compound is colorless, but samples tend to acquire a yellow cast over time through decomposition into oxides of [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]]. Most commercial nitric acid is a 68% solution in water; solutions containing more than 86% HNO₃ are called fuming nitric acid. It is the primary reagent for nitration, the addition of a nitro group, typically to an organic molecule. Some resulting nitro compounds are [[Explosive|explosives]], a few are stable enough for munitions and demolition, and others serve as synthetic dyes and medicines. It is also a strong oxidizing agent. Industrial production from air began in 1905 with the Birkeland–Eyde arc process, but most output now comes from the Ostwald process, which oxidizes [[Ammonia|ammonia]]. About 70–80% of production is used to make [[Ammonium nitrate|ammonium nitrate]] and other [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]].

Colorless gas with the formula NO, one of the principal oxides of [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]]. It is a free radical with an unpaired electron, and a heteronuclear diatomic molecule whose study helped inspire early theories of chemical bonding. Nitric oxide forms in combustion systems and is generated by [[Lightning|lightning]] in thunderstorms. [[Joseph Priestley]] first identified it in the late 18th century, when it was seen as a toxic byproduct of combustion. In mammals it acts as a signaling molecule, and the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded for discovering its role in the cardiovascular system. Its applications include the development of [[Sildenafil|sildenafil]] (Viagra) and use in [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] manufacturing.

Highly flammable compound formed by nitrating [[Cellulose|cellulose]] with a mixture of [[Nitric acid|nitric]] and [[Sulfuric acid|sulfuric acids]]. Also known as cellulose nitrate, guncotton or flash paper, depending on form. Nitrocellulose was an early replacement for [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]] as a propellant in [[Firearm|firearms]] and as a low-order explosive in mining. As collodion, it was a critical component of early photographic emulsions that revolutionized [[Photography|photography]] in the 1860s. In the 20th century it was adapted to automobile lacquers and adhesives. Its principal uses are lacquers and coatings, explosives and celluloid; nail polish also contains it.

Dense, oily [[Explosive|explosive]] liquid, usually produced by nitrating [[Glycerol|glycerol]] with white fuming [[Nitric acid|nitric acid]]. Chemically it is a nitrate ester rather than a nitro compound, though the traditional name is retained. Ascanio Sobrero discovered it, and [[Alfred Nobel]] reduced its instability by absorbing it into diatomaceous earth to form [[Dynamite]], which is used in construction, demolition and mining. Nitroglycerin is extremely sensitive to shock, heat and rough handling, and its instability caused numerous industrial accidents. Since 1878 it has also been used as a medication, a potent vasodilator that treats angina pectoris and chronic [[Heart failure|heart failure]].

Colorless, non-flammable [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]] (N₂O), commonly known as laughing gas. At elevated temperatures it is a powerful oxidizer, similar to molecular oxygen. It is widely used as an anesthetic and pain reliever in surgery and dentistry, and it is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. [[Humphry Davy]] coined the name "laughing gas" for its euphoric effects. It is also used as an oxidizer in [[Rocket|rocket]] propellants and motor racing fuels, and as a frothing gas for whipped cream. Chronic recreational abuse may cause neurological damage through inactivation of [[Vitamin B12|vitamin B₁₂]]. Its atmospheric concentration was 340 parts per billion (ppb) in 2026, rising about 1 ppb a year, and about 40% of human-caused emissions come from [[Agriculture|agriculture]], where soil microorganisms convert nitrogen fertilizers into it. It is the third most important greenhouse gas.

Self-governing island country (pop., 2022: 1,689) in the South Pacific Ocean, in Polynesia, in free association with [[New Zealand|New Zealand]]. Niue lies 2,400 km northeast of New Zealand and covers about 261.46 sq km. It is one of the world's largest coral islands and is nicknamed "The Rock." A [[Limestone|limestone]] cliff runs along the coast, and a central plateau rises about 60 m above sea level, surrounded by a [[Coral reef|coral reef]]. Niueans are citizens of New Zealand, and [[Charles III]] is head of state as King of New Zealand. Niue is a parliamentary democracy divided into 14 villages. It is not a member of the [[United Nations]], but it belongs to some UN specialized agencies, such as [[UNESCO]]. [[James Cook]] reached the island in 1774 and named it "Savage Island"; its original name, Niue, later regained use. The economy has centered on [[Subsistence agriculture|subsistence agriculture]], with emerging tourism, postage-stamp revenue and substantial New Zealand aid.

Persian Sunni scholar, jurist and vizier of the [[Seljuk Empire|Seljuk Empire]]. Rising from a low position in the empire, he became the de facto ruler of the realm for 20 years after the assassination of Sultan Alp Arslan in 1072. Persianate historical traditions portray him as the archetypal "good vizier," and he is widely regarded as one of the most influential statesmen in medieval Islamic history. He founded a system of madrasas across the Seljuk Empire, called the Nizamiyya after him, which advanced Shafi'i jurisprudence and Ash'ari theology. He is traditionally credited with the *Siyasatnama* (*Book of Government*), a treatise that uses historical anecdotes to discuss justice, effective rule and the role of the bureaucracy. Born near Tus in [[Khorasan|Khorasan]], he became chief administrator of the entire Khorasan province by 1059.

Persian poet, considered the greatest romantic epic poet in [[Persian literature|Persian literature]]. He was born in Ganja, in the Seljuk Empire, now in Azerbaijan, and is believed to have spent his whole life in the South Caucasus. Orphaned early, he was raised by his maternal uncle, who gave him an excellent education. He was not a court poet, so few facts about his life are known beyond his own work. He is often called Hakim ("the Sage"). His *Khamsa* (*Quintet*) comprises five interconnected [[Masnavi|masnavi]] epics, composed between 1183 and 1197, including *Khosrow and Shirin*, *Layla and Majnun* and *Haft Peykar* (*Seven Beauties*). He brought a colloquial and realistic style to the Persian epic. Modern Azerbaijani writers sometimes present him as Turkic, but scholars generally place him in the Persian-Iranian cultural milieu.

City (pop., 2024: 1,205,000) and administrative center of Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, in central Russia. It lies at the confluence of the Oka and [[Volga|Volga]] rivers, 420 km east of Moscow, and is the second-most populous city on the Volga. Prince George II of Vladimir founded it on February 4, 1221. In 1612 Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky organized an army that liberated Moscow from Polish and Lithuanian forces. The city became a major trade center of the Russian Empire in 1817. From 1932 to 1990 it was called Gorky, after the author [[Maxim Gorky|Maxim Gorky]], who was born there, and the Gorky Automobile Plant made it an industrial center. The metro opened in 1985, and the city was one of the host cities of the 2018 [[FIFA|FIFA]] World Cup.

Nigerian nationalist and politician, the first native governor-general of Nigeria (1960–1963) and its first president (1963–1966). Known as "Zik of Africa," he is widely regarded as the father of Nigerian nationalism. Born in Zungeru to Igbo parents from Onitsha, he learned Hausa as a child, then Igbo in Onitsha and Yoruba in Lagos. He studied in the United States at Storer College, [[Columbia University|Columbia University]], the University of Pennsylvania and Howard University. He was introduced to the teachings of [[Marcus Garvey|Marcus Garvey]], which became part of his nationalist rhetoric. Azikiwe worked as a journalist in the Gold Coast and in 1937 founded the *West African Pilot*. He co-founded the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons in 1944 and was premier of Eastern Nigeria from 1954 to 1959. His presidency ended in a 1966 military coup. His endorsement of Biafran secession during the 1967–1970 civil war highlighted tensions in his commitment to national unity.

American lexicographer and textbook author, known for *An American Dictionary of the English Language* (1828). Webster graduated from Yale College in 1778 and, after finding little work as a lawyer, built his finances on a private school and educational books, including the *Blue-Back Speller*, which taught generations of American children to spell and read. A strong supporter of the American Revolution and of the ratification of the Constitution, he was recruited in 1793 by [[Alexander Hamilton|Alexander Hamilton]] to edit a [[Federalist Party|Federalist]] newspaper in [[New York City|New York City]]. His first dictionary appeared in 1806, and the expanded 1828 work popularized distinctly American spellings. He contributed to the Copyright Act of 1831, the first major statutory revision of U.S. [[Copyright|copyright]] law. He has been called the "Father of American Scholarship and Education."

Biblical patriarch, the last of the antediluvian patriarchs in [[Abrahamic religions|Abrahamic traditions]], known for building an ark. In the [[Book of Genesis|Book of Genesis]], God decides to punish human evil with a flood, and Noah builds the ark at God's command to save his family and the land animals. Afterward God makes a covenant with Noah never again to destroy the earth by flood, and the rainbow is set in the clouds as its pledge. Noah is also portrayed as the first to cultivate the vine. His story also appears in the [[Quran|Quran]]. Most scholars suggest the biblical account was influenced by earlier Mesopotamian traditions, notably the [[Epic of Gilgamesh|Epic of Gilgamesh]], composed around 1800 BC, in which a hero builds an ark to survive a divine flood.

American linguist, philosopher and political critic, sometimes called the "father of modern linguistics." His landmark work *Syntactic Structures* (1957) remodeled the study of language. He developed generative grammar, universal grammar and the Chomsky hierarchy, and he helped spark the cognitive revolution in the human sciences. He was particularly critical of [[Behaviorism|behaviorism]] and the work of [[B. F. Skinner|B. F. Skinner]]. He taught at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] and is an institute professor emeritus there, and he is a laureate professor at the University of Arizona. He has written more than 150 books. An outspoken opponent of the [[Vietnam War|Vietnam War]], he rose to national attention in 1967 with the essay "The Responsibility of Intellectuals." His defense of unconditional [[Freedom of speech|free speech]], including that of Holocaust denial, generated controversy in the Faurisson affair of the 1980s. He is a leading critic of U.S. foreign policy and [[Capitalism|capitalism]], and he argues that Israel's treatment of Palestinians is worse than South African-style [[Apartheid|apartheid]].

Annual international prizes established by the will of [[Alfred Nobel|Alfred Nobel]] in 1895. The original prizes cover [[Physics|physics]], [[Chemistry|chemistry]], [[Medicine|physiology or medicine]], [[Literature|literature]] and [[Peace|peace]]. A sixth, the Prize in Economic Sciences, was established in 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank (Sweden's central bank) in Nobel's memory. Nobel's fortune came largely from his 355 inventions, most famously [[Dynamite|dynamite]]. His will directed that his estate fund prizes for those who confer the "greatest benefit on mankind." The Nobel Foundation administers the prizes, which were first awarded in 1901. Except in unusual circumstances such as war, all six prizes are given annually. Each laureate receives a gold medal, a diploma and a monetary award; as of 2023 the award was 11,000,000 kr, about US$1,035,000. No more than three individuals may share a prize.

Social class ranked immediately below royalty in societies with an aristocracy. Membership is typically hereditary and patrilineal, and it carries titles such as "Prince," "Lord" or "Lady," along with privileges that vary by country and era. Monarchs or governments historically granted nobility, though wealth, power or royal favor occasionally allowed commoners to rise. In feudal Europe, nobles held fiefs in exchange for military and other services to a sovereign, and the status became hereditary, sometimes with fiscal privileges, as in pre-revolutionary [[France|France]]. The nobiles of the [[Roman Republic|Roman Republic]] were families descended from men who had reached the consulship. By the 21st century, noble status had become largely honorary in most societies, though some privileges remain legally in countries such as Spain and the United Kingdom. More than a third of British land is held by aristocrats and traditional landed gentry.

Group 18 of the periodic table, a set of low-reactive, gaseous chemical elements. [[Helium|Helium]], neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are odorless, colorless, monatomic gases with cryogenic boiling points below 165 K. Their weak London dispersion forces and full outer shells of [[Electron shell|valence electrons]] make them largely unreactive, although a few hundred compounds are known. [[Oganesson|Oganesson]], an unstable synthetic element whose properties are uncertain, is sometimes included. [[Argon|Argon]] shields [[Welding|welding]] and fills [[Incandescent light bulb|incandescent bulbs]], helium provides buoyancy for blimps and balloons, and helium and neon serve as refrigerants. Industrial supplies come from separating air by liquefaction and fractional distillation, except for radon, which is isolated from the radioactive decay of radium, thorium or uranium compounds. The term "noble gas" was introduced in 1900 by Hugo Erdmann, by analogy with noble metals.

Series of 21 nocturnes for solo [[Piano|piano]] by [[Frédéric Chopin|Frédéric Chopin]], generally considered among the finest short solo works for the instrument. Chopin did not invent the nocturne but popularized and expanded the form developed by the Irish composer John Field. He kept Field's song-like right-hand melody over broken chords in the left hand and heavier use of the pedal, but used a freer rhythm and developed the structure under the influence of Italian and French opera [[Aria|arias]] and sonata form. He also used [[Counterpoint|counterpoint]] to create tension. Nocturnes 1 to 18 were published during his lifetime; numbers 19 and 20 were written earlier but published posthumously. Number 21 was not originally titled a nocturne, but it has been included in the set since its 1938 publication. Early reviews were mixed, and many critics later reversed their judgments.

Statement that every continuous symmetry of the action of a physical system with conservative forces has a corresponding conservation law. [[Emmy Noether|Emmy Noether]] published it in 1918 as the first of two theorems. The action is the time integral of a Lagrangian function. Rotational symmetry implies conservation of angular momentum, time-translation symmetry implies conservation of energy, and spatial-translation symmetry implies conservation of linear momentum. The theorem is used in theoretical physics and the calculus of variations. It does not apply to systems that cannot be modeled with a Lagrangian alone, such as dissipative systems.

Classical Japanese dance-drama, performed since the 14th century. Noh is Japan's oldest major theater art still regularly performed. Its plays are often based on tales in which a supernatural being, transformed into a human hero, narrates the story. Performers use [[Mask|masks]], costumes and props in a highly trained, stylized dance-based performance, and the iemoto system codifies its traditions. Traditional nōgaku programs placed several Noh plays with comic kyōgen pieces between them, while an abbreviated program of two Noh plays and one kyōgen piece is common today. Noh evolved from [[Performing arts|performing arts]] such as sarugaku. Kan'ami Kiyotsugu and his son [[Zeami Motokiyo|Zeami Motokiyo]] refined it, and with the patronage of [[Shogun|shogun]] Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, Zeami established Noh as the leading theater art of its time.

Chiefly unwanted, unintentional or harmful sound that is unpleasant, loud or disruptive to hearing or mental faculties. From a physics standpoint, noise and desired sound are both vibrations through a medium; the difference lies in how the brain perceives them. Sound is measured by amplitude, expressed in [[Decibel|decibels]] (dB), and by frequency, expressed in [[Hertz|hertz]] (Hz). Noise is often measured in dBA using A-weighting, where 0 dBA is the softest sound a person can hear, normal speech is about 65 dBA, and a rock concert can reach about 120 dBA. In audio engineering, noise also means residual hiss, rumble, crackle or hum, and in experimental science it denotes random fluctuations that obscure a signal. Environmental noise from road vehicles, aircraft, trains and industry causes annoyance and disrupted sleep, and it is linked to [[Hearing loss|hearing loss]] and cardiovascular disease.

Ancient civilization of central [[Nigeria|Nigeria]], named after the village of Nok in southern Kaduna State, where its terracotta sculptures were discovered in 1928. Nok culture may have emerged around 1500 BCE and persisted until about 1 BCE. Its people may have produced terracotta sculptures on a large scale as part of a complex funerary culture. The earliest sculptures may date to 900 BCE, and some figures wield slingshots, bows and arrows, which may indicate hunting. A sculpture of two paddlers in a dugout canoe suggests river transport along tributaries of the [[Niger River|Niger River]] and regional [[Trade|trade]]. Nok sculptures are regarded as the earliest large three-dimensional figurative art in continental Africa, excluding ancient Egyptian art. Iron metallurgy may have developed independently between 750 BCE and 550 BCE, and settlements are often found on mountaintops.

Finnish multinational telecommunications and consumer electronics corporation, originally established as a pulp mill in 1865 in the Tampere region. For a decade beginning in 1998, Nokia was the largest worldwide [[Mobile phone|mobile phone]] vendor, but after poor management decisions its market share fell sharply. In 2014 [[Microsoft|Microsoft]] bought its mobile phone business. Nokia then focused on telecommunications infrastructure and the Internet of things, acquiring Alcatel-Lucent, including its [[Bell Labs|Bell Labs]] research organization. The Nokia brand returned to phones in 2016 under a licensing arrangement with HMD. Nokia remains a major patent licensor and, as of 2018, was the world's third-largest network equipment manufacturer.

Member of a community without fixed habitation that regularly moves to and from areas. Nomadic groups include [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherers]], pastoral nomads who keep [[Livestock|livestock]], and itinerant craftspeople and traders. Nomadic hunting and gathering is by far the oldest known human subsistence method. Pastoralists move their herds in patterns that avoid depleting pastures, and mobility suits [[Steppe|steppe]], [[Tundra|tundra]] and desert environments, where many groups are reindeer herders. A [[Mongolia|Mongolian]] family moves twice a year, between summer and winter pastures. Most nomads travel in groups of families, bands or tribes, and a council of adult males makes most decisions. As of 1995, an estimated 30–40 million nomads lived worldwide, a population that declined slowly through the 20th century.

Forum of 120 countries not formally aligned with or against any major power bloc. Founded in 1961 in [[Belgrade|Belgrade]], Yugoslavia, it drew on principles from the 1955 Bandung Conference. Leaders including [[Josip Broz Tito|Josip Broz Tito]], Gamal Abdel Nasser, Jawaharlal Nehru, Kwame Nkrumah and Sukarno formed it during the [[Cold War|Cold War]], as a counterweight to the pro-Soviet bloc, whose best known alliance was the [[Warsaw Pact|Warsaw Pact]], and to the pro-American bloc, many of whose members belonged to [[NATO|NATO]]. Its members make up nearly two-thirds of the [[United Nations|United Nations]] and contain 55% of the world population. After the UN, it is the largest grouping of states worldwide.

Pair of geometries based on axioms closely related to those specifying [[Euclidean geometry|Euclidean geometry]]. Non-Euclidean geometry arises by replacing [[Euclid|Euclid]]'s parallel postulate with an alternative. In hyperbolic geometry, infinitely many lines through a point not on a given line fail to intersect it, and the lines diverge; in elliptic geometry, every such line intersects the given line, and lines converge. Mathematicians tried for at least a thousand years to prove the parallel postulate from the other four, including [[Ibn al-Haytham|Ibn al-Haytham]] and Omar Khayyám. Lobachevsky published the first rigorous non-Euclidean system in 1829–1830, and Bolyai formulated a similar one in 1832. Non-Euclidean geometry underpins Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity (1915), in which spacetime is modeled as a curved [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian manifold]].
